issues: Minor, form only: 'a checkup that finds nothing year after year, and no sick days in years' says 'year(s)' twice in the closing eight words; one occurrence carries the standing-constitution sense. Body-only, faithful and in range otherwise.
entries.suggested_edit: This means having a sound constitution: shaking off whatever is going around in a day, no prescriptions, a clean checkup every time, and no sick days in years.

issues: Scope mismatch with its partner: good_looking gives one clause of the body itself ('even features and clear skin') before the reception clauses; plain_looking gives reception only (no compliments, ordinary photographs, features nobody remembers). Add the body clause so the pair matches in scope; the suggested text keeps the length at 31 against 30.
entries.suggested_edit: This means having a face and figure nobody looks at twice: unremarkable features, no compliments on one's looks, photographs that come out ordinary, and a face nobody remembers after one meeting.

sets.name: athletic / sedentary
sets.review: One grain: the daily activity level and its results in the body (pulse or wind on the stairs, muscle or softness, stiffness). The activity clauses ('training most days', 'driving to the corner store') are the trait itself, as the packet allows; no character word on either pole. Lengths 30 / 31.

sets.name: hair colour set
sets.review: One grain across the five: the colour range, brows and lashes or freckles, and how the hair meets sun, gray and dye, each member taking a different one of those particulars. No temperament anywhere (nothing fiery, carefree or dull). Red hair carries freckles and sunburn as the packet asks; the sunburn overlap with fair_skinned is a fact of the body and acceptable. gray_haired states the years as a fact of the hair and stops. Two optional points for Roger: (a) black_haired is the only member whose opening dodges the colour word ('hair so dark it shows blue in strong light') while the eye set names its colours outright; 'having black hair that shows blue in strong light' would be more even, but the dodge is also fine and the sheen clause does identify the colour. (b) 'blonde' and 'brunette' are the feminine forms in English ('blond' is the masculine), so the generator may skew those two toward women; a label question, not a draft fault.

sets.name: eye colour set
sets.review: One grain: the colour range, the eye in bright sun, and how the colour reads. Naming the colour in the opening is right: the colour is the whole content, there is no non-echoing way to say which eyes, and the rule-1 case (a behaviour already glossed by the label) does not arise. green_eyed and the jealousy idiom: 'having green eyes' picks the sense and nothing later points at envy. Small asymmetry: brown and green each carry a frequency clause ('the world's commonest eye color', 'a color few share') and blue none; harmless. Lengths 29 / 31 / 29.

sets.name: dark_skinned / fair_skinned
sets.review: One grain: skin and sun, the foundation shade, how a rash reads, one medical consequence each (vitamin D / SPF). Neither pole touches race, country or social experience, and the heritage memberships stay the place for that. Wince test on dark_skinned passes: the foundation hunt, the purple rash and winter vitamin D are what a dark-skinned adult would say of their own body. 'Deepening in summer sun without burning' is a shade absolute (dark skin burns less readily, not never), as is the fair pole's 'twenty minutes'; both are plain generalisations of the kind the corpus uses and I would leave them. Lengths 32 / 30.

sets.name: good_looking / plain_looking
sets.review: Grain is how the face and figure are received, which the packet allows for this pair; no vanity, confidence or shyness on either side, and plain_looking is an opposite (ordinary, unremarked, forgotten), not an absence. The one mismatch is scope: good_looking has a body clause ('even features and clear skin') that plain_looking lacks; the suggested edit adds 'unremarkable features'. Lengths 30 / 28 (31 with the edit).

sets.name: healthy / sickly
sets.review: One grain through the same four markers on both poles (what is going around, prescriptions, the checkup, sick days); standing constitution on both, not a current illness, and sickly is not softened (weeks to shake a bug, something found at the checkup, sick days used up by spring) nor turned into hypochondria. The suggested healthy edit is cosmetic (the doubled 'year'). Lengths 31 / 31 (28 / 31 with the edit).

sets.name: constitution and chronic conditions (not an arrangement)
sets.review: The three stay apart as the notes require: sickly is a weak constitution (many minor illnesses, slowly thrown off), chronically_ill is one long-term illness that is managed (medication, specialists, flares), in_chronic_pain is pain from injury or wear (back, joints, old injury; painkillers, heating pad, broken sleep) with no illness named. Each has its duration written in ('for weeks' and 'by spring'; 'for years'; 'every day for years'). The patient role stays the acute case.

sets.name: heavyset / slender
sets.review: One grain: the build and its practicalities (sizes, the fit of seats, body temperature); neutral words, no cause (eating, dieting), no feeling about it. slender has four particulars to heavyset's three (the belt clause has no counterpart); lengths 27 / 30, both in range, so acceptable as is. If Roger wants them even, 'a belt let out to the last hole' would be the counterpart.

sets.name: short / tall
sets.review: One grain, mirrored openings ('a head below / above most people') and practicalities of reach, clothes, crowd or doorway, seat. short's opening picks the height sense over 'curt', so no qualifier is needed; no Napoleon clause, no assertiveness or shyness. tall's 'being asked to reach the top shelf' is correctly something the body meets, not a helpful disposition. Lengths 30 / 32.

sets.name: female / male
sets.review: One grain through parallel markers: reproductive anatomy, the cycle or the puberty changes, carrying a child or muscle on the frame, the sex-specific screening. Bodily sex only; nothing on roles, family or temperament, and clear of the expression set (feminine carries warmth and masculine toughness, which neither draft touches). On the writer's question: the plainness is right. 'Ovaries, a uterus and breasts', 'testes and a penis', periods, menopause, Pap smears, mammograms, prostate checks are the ordinary adult words, neither clinical ('genitalia', 'reproductive organs') nor coarse. One optional word: 'testicles' is slightly more everyday than 'testes'; either passes. 'A woman's body' / 'a man's body' is the right gloss (the alternative 'female body' echoes the label). Lengths 32 / 32.

sets.name: roles: athlete, pregnant
sets.review: athlete: the training, the season, the body as instrument, the injury; no 'driven' or 'competitive'; properly apart from gym_rat (lifting, no competition), competitor (rivalry as a disposition), coach and trainer (develop others), surfer and daredevil. pregnant: the months of the body changing, the appointments, the due date; no mood stereotype (no glow, no hormones, no nesting). On 'A pregnant woman is someone' against the corpus's 'A <adj> person is someone' (homeless, unemployed, estranged): I side with the writer. The packet's standard for the body is 'as an adult would say it of themselves', and a pregnant woman says 'pregnant woman'; 'A pregnant person' is a one-word swap if Roger prefers the pattern, and the choice is his. Both 41 words, in the role range.

summary:
28 drafts read against the body-only rule, the notes and the form: no draft carries a personality, temper, attitude or behaviour clause beyond the physical activity it is about, and no stereotype rides in on a particular (freckles and sunburn for red hair, light sensitivity for blue eyes, the years as a fact of gray hair). All 26 traits are one sentence of 27 to 32 words and both roles 41; US spelling throughout; no partner or neighbour named.
Two edits, both small: plain_looking lacks the body clause its partner has ('even features and clear skin'), so the pair's scope is uneven, and a text with 'unremarkable features' is given; healthy says 'year(s)' twice in its last eight words, cosmetic, text given. Everything else is ok; nearest-existing lines are plausible for all 28 (checked energetic, lethargic, health_conscious / health_negligent, body_confident / body_insecure, feminine / masculine, elderly / middle_aged, envious, short_term_oriented, blind, patient, gym_rat, competitor, surfer, homeless / unemployed / estranged) and no duplicate exists; no height, hair, eye, skin, sex, sport or pregnancy entity is in the corpus today.
On the writer's questions: the anatomy words in male and female are at the right plainness (optional: 'testicles' for 'testes'); naming the colour in the eye-set openings is right and unavoidable; green_eyed, short_sighted and short each pick the physical sense in the opening; the red-hair / fair-skin sunburn overlap is a fact of the body and acceptable; sickly, chronically_ill and in_chronic_pain are properly apart; 'A pregnant woman is someone' is the better reading of the body-as-lived rule, with 'A pregnant person' the one-word fallback for Roger to choose.
For Roger, label-level and optional: 'short-sighted' is the British term (US 'nearsighted'), the same spelling question that renamed gray_haired; 'blonde' and 'brunette' are the feminine forms and may skew generation toward women; black_haired is the only colour member whose opening does not name its colour.
